subject: biology
topicDisplay: Theme A · Organisms & Ecosystems (Diversity, Classification, Evolution, Conservation)
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the binomial naming system, the correct way to write the human species name is:
questions.explain: The genus (Homo) is capitalised and the species epithet (sapiens) is lower case; both are italicised.

questions.q: A species is most usefully defined as a group of organisms that:
options: Can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
questions.explain: The biological species concept centres on the ability to interbreed and produce fertile offspring, though it has limitations.

questions.q: A dichotomous key identifies an organism by:
options: A series of paired, contrasting choices
questions.explain: At each step the user selects between two contrasting descriptions, narrowing down to the organism's identity.

questions.q: Biodiversity includes species diversity, ecosystem diversity and:
questions.explain: Biodiversity spans genetic variation within species, the variety of species, and the range of ecosystems.

questions.q: A clade is defined as:
options: A common ancestor together with all of its descendants
A group sharing an analogous structure
questions.explain: Clades (monophyletic groups) are the basis of modern natural classification.

questions.q: Modern cladograms are increasingly constructed using:
options: Base and amino acid sequence data
questions.explain: Molecular (sequence) data give objective evidence of relatedness and have led to reclassification of some groups.

questions.q: The pentadactyl (five-fingered) limb of mammals, birds and amphibians is an example of a homologous structure, providing evidence of:
questions.explain: Shared underlying structure with different functions indicates descent from a common ancestor and adaptive radiation.

questions.q: The wings of insects and the wings of birds perform the same function but have different origins. They are:
options: Analogous structures produced by convergent evolution
questions.explain: Analogous structures arise when unrelated organisms independently evolve similar adaptations to similar selection pressures.

questions.q: Natural selection requires all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Darwinian selection acts on heritable variation and overproduction of offspring; the inheritance of acquired characteristics (Lamarckism) is not part of it.

questions.q: The spread of antibiotic resistance in bacterial populations is a real-world example of:
questions.explain: Antibiotics select for pre-existing resistant variants, which survive and reproduce, increasing resistance frequency.

questions.q: Allopatric speciation is driven initially by:
questions.explain: A physical barrier separates populations, which then diverge until they can no longer interbreed.

questions.q: Speciation by polyploidy, common in plants, is a mechanism of:
questions.explain: Polyploidy can create reproductive isolation within the same geographic area, producing new species without physical separation.

questions.q: Which of the following provides direct fossil-independent evidence for evolution?
questions.explain: Artificial selection shows how heritable change accumulates rapidly under selection, supporting the mechanism of evolution.

questions.q: Two populations are considered separate species once they show:
questions.explain: When populations can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, speciation is complete.

questions.q: In-situ conservation means conserving species:
questions.explain: In-situ conservation (e.g. nature reserves, national parks) protects species within functioning ecosystems.

questions.q: Which is an example of ex-situ conservation?
questions.explain: Ex-situ methods (zoos, botanic gardens, seed and sperm banks) conserve organisms outside their natural habitat.

questions.q: A keystone species is one that:
options: Has a disproportionately large effect on its community relative to its abundance
Is always the most numerous species
Cannot be removed from a food web
questions.explain: Removing a keystone species (e.g. sea otters) can cause large changes in community structure.

questions.q: The single biggest current cause of biodiversity loss worldwide is:
questions.explain: Habitat loss and fragmentation (from land-use change) is the leading driver of the current biodiversity crisis, alongside climate change and overexploitation.

questions.q: The EDGE of Existence programme prioritises species that are:
questions.explain: EDGE targets species that are both highly distinct on the tree of life and at high risk of extinction.

questions.q: Ongoing monitoring shows biodiversity is declining. A valid line of evidence for a biodiversity crisis is:
options: Rising rates of species extinction above background levels
A stable number of described species
Constant population sizes of threatened species
questions.explain: Extinction rates well above the natural background rate, plus falling population and habitat indices, evidence the crisis.
